title: the teacher on the bed of arrows
hook: the man who won the war wants to walk away from the throne, so Krishna takes him to the grandfather he brought down
carry: parampara: wisdom handed down, person to person

segments.voice: Yesterday Stri ended at the river, where Kunti told her sons that Karna was their brother. Your line was tarpan, water for every one we lost.

Yudhishthira has everything he fought for, and he doesn't want any of it. The kingdom is his. His enemies are gone. And he tells his brothers he's leaving for the forest, to live as a hermit. A kingdom bought with the deaths of teachers, cousins and a brother he never knew is not something he can bear to rule. His brothers argue. Draupadi argues. Sages come and argue, and at last he lets himself be crowned. But the grief and doubt don't leave him. So Krishna takes him to the field, to the one teacher still alive there: Bhishma, lying on his bed of arrows.
screen: `HE WON, AND WANTS TO LEAVE.` → `NOBODY CAN MOVE HIM.` → `KRISHNA TAKES HIM TO BHISHMA.`

segments.voice: The next two books, Shanti, peace, and Anushasana, instruction, are mostly one long conversation, and the peace sought is Yudhishthira's own. The surprise is who teaches. Krishna is there, and Krishna is God in this story. Yet he steps back. He gives Bhishma relief, so the pain of the arrows, the weariness and the confusion leave him, and his mind becomes clear. Bhishma asks, in effect, why not teach him yourself? Krishna's answer, in Ganguli's telling: he wants these words to come from Bhishma, so that Bhishma's fame will last as long as the world does. Then there's Yudhishthira. He hangs back, ashamed. His side brought this old man down. Bhishma has to call him forward and tell him he has nothing to fear. And God stands to one side. Many teachers read the scene as a picture of what Hindus call parampara: wisdom handed down, teacher to student, person to person. In the Gita, Krishna says this knowledge came down through a line of teachers, and tells Arjuna how to receive it: bow, ask your questions, serve, and the wise will teach you. Yudhishthira has to do exactly that: walk up, ashamed, and ask. Today, the person who could teach you most may be the one you're most shy to approach.
screen: `SHANTI: PEACE. ANUSHASANA: INSTRUCTION.` · `KRISHNA GIVES BHISHMA CLARITY` · `YUDHISHTHIRA HANGS BACK` · then, large: `PARAMPARA: HANDED DOWN`

segments.voice: Hindus often bow to a teacher before learning, and touch an elder's feet for a blessing. Join your palms and bow your head a little. Picture yourself sitting beside one person who taught you something real, a parent, a teacher, a friend, an elder. Breathe in and let one question you'd ask them now come up, with any shame or distance that's there too; you don't need the answer. If you pray, you can hold that person and your question in your prayer. If you don't, simply hold the question.
Shanti. Peace: the book where Bhishma teaches Yudhishthira from the bed of arrows, and Krishna steps back to let him.
Your line: parampara, wisdom handed down, person to person. Tomorrow, what Bhishma says a king is for. Day eight hundred sixty-one.

howItsDone: Hindu teachers read the Shanti Parva and Anushasana Parva as a storehouse of teaching on duty, kingship and freedom, and the scene of Yudhishthira at Bhishma's side is painted and retold as a picture of parampara, wisdom passed from teacher to student.
